title: Glacier mass balance and the retreating snout
text:
A glacier is commonly described as a river of ice, and the analogy is more accurate than it first appears, provided you understand what is flowing and why. Snow falls in the upper reaches, where more accumulates each winter than melts each summer. It compacts under its own weight, the air is squeezed out, and over years it becomes dense glacial ice. Once that ice is thick enough, it deforms under gravity and begins to creep downhill, and where meltwater lubricates the bed it can also slide.

The key idea is mass balance. The upper part of a glacier is the accumulation zone, where it gains ice; the lower part, warmer because it lies at lower altitude, is the ablation zone, where it loses ice to melting. Between them sits a boundary called the equilibrium line. If gains and losses match over a year, the glacier's snout stays roughly where it is. Notice the consequence. A retreating glacier is not a glacier that has stopped moving. The ice continues to flow forwards; it is simply melting back faster than it is delivered. Worldwide, most glaciers are now losing more than they gain, and their snouts are retreating uphill.
points: A glacier forms where snow accumulates and compacts under its own weight into dense ice, which then deforms and creeps downhill under gravity, sometimes sliding on meltwater.
Mass balance is the key concept: the upper accumulation zone gains ice and the lower, warmer ablation zone loses it to melting.
The boundary between the two is the equilibrium line, and when gains match losses the glacier's snout stays in place.
A retreating glacier has not stopped moving; the ice still flows forwards but melts back faster than it is supplied.
Most glaciers worldwide are now losing more ice than they gain and their snouts are retreating uphill.
